sections.skill: Strategy: mark the route as you trace it
sections.relationship: Students lose track in a busy network or miscount routes. Tracing with a finger and writing the towns in order, and listing routes in a fixed order, makes counts complete.
sections.author_note: Students lose track in a busy network or miscount routes. Tracing with a finger and writing the towns in order, and listing routes in a fixed order, makes counts complete.

lesson.title: Mark the route as you trace it
text: Write each route as a list of towns, for example A-B-D.
To count routes, list them in a fixed order: all routes starting A-B first, then those starting A-C, and so on. Never revisit a town in the same route if the rule forbids it.
For the shortest route, find all towns 1 road away, then all towns 2 roads away, and so on.
For a walk that uses every road once, count roads at each town: it is possible only if 0 or 2 towns have an odd number of roads (and the network is all one piece).

example.title: Worked example (a different network)
prompt: Towns W, X, Y, Z with roads W-X, X-Y, Y-Z, W-Y. How many routes from W to Z without repeating a town?
steps: Routes must end with Y-Z, because Z only touches Y.
From W to Y: W-Y, or W-X-Y.
So the routes are W-Y-Z and W-X-Y-Z: 2 routes.

questions.prompt: A network has towns with these numbers of roads: 3, 3, 2, 2 and k. For a walk that uses every road exactly once to be possible in a connected network, at most two towns may have an odd number of roads. Give a whole number k from 1 to 6 that keeps this possible.
questions.rule: (isEven(k) and k >= 1 and k <= 6) and isInteger(k) and k >= 0
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: (isEven(k) and k >= 1 and k <= 6) and isInteger(k) and k >= 0 (example: k = 2)
